verdict.rationale: Both replace the quadratic findIndex scan with a Map from normalized email to first index, preserve first-match semantics and arrival order, and add the same duplicate-in-existing test. B is a little more straightforward: it normalizes each incoming email once and records the new index explicitly. A normalizes twice for new contacts and hides the index inside `result.push(contact) - 1`. B also adds a scale test that checks count and ordering as well as speed; its 2 s timing bound is a mild flakiness risk but has a wide margin.
a_issues: `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` is a compact, clever expression that is harder to read than an explicit index.
Each new incoming email is normalized twice: once for the lookup and again inside `remember`.
Nothing in the suite guards against a return to quadratic behaviour; the benchmark was run once and deleted.
b_issues: The wall-clock assertion (`elapsed < 2000`) could fail on very slow or overloaded CI machines.
The report does not say the new output was compared against the old implementation on the same data; it relies on reasoning plus tests.

verdict.rationale: Both changes make the same correct fix: a Map from normalized email to the first index, updated as new contacts are appended. Behavior is preserved, including first-match merging when the stored book already has duplicates. A is slightly more direct to read, normalizes each email only once, and adds a scale test that checks both correctness and performance with a generous threshold. B's report is more rigorous, with a before/after measurement and a check of its new test against the old code, but B leaves no regression guard for the performance fix.
a_issues: The wall-clock timing assertion could in principle flake on very slow CI, though a 2 s limit against roughly 68 ms is generous.
The report says the output is identical to before without saying this was checked against the old implementation.
b_issues: The `remember` closure combined with `result.push(contact) - 1` is a bit clever and harder to read than an explicit index.
Newly appended contacts get their email normalized twice, once for the lookup and again inside `remember`.
No test protects the performance improvement, which was the whole point of the task.
